title: Optimization of Guava Leaf Extract Loading in Chitosan–STTP Microencapsulation for Inhibition of Pyrite Oxidation

authors.name: Ernik Dwi Safitria
authors.affiliation: Department of Physics, Faculty of Science and Mathematics, Diponegoro University

abstract: Guava (Psidium guajava L.) leaf extract contains tannins, phenolics and flavonoids that inhibit oxidative degradation of sulfide minerals. However, direct use of extracts suffers from rapid leaching and limited durability under aqueous oxidative conditions. This work investigates ionic-gelation microencapsulation of ultrasonically extracted guava leaf extract (GLE) in chitosan matrices cross-linked with sodium tripolyphosphate (STTP) to optimize extract loading for pyrite (FeS2) oxidation inhibition. Extract concentrations between $500$ and $8000$ ppm were evaluated. Optimal loading in the range $2000$--$3500$ ppm produced microcapsules of $315$--$390$ nm and polydispersity index $\mathrm{PDI}<0.5$. Leaching tests (48 h, oxidative solution) and ICP-OES quantification show sulfur reduction from $24.94$ mg/L (uncoated) to $5.94$ mg/L (microencapsulated), and iron reduction from $18.20$ mg/L to $3.80$ mg/L, indicating improved inhibition and controlled release. The method, implemented at Diponegoro University laboratories, offers a scalable, eco-friendly inhibition approach for pyrite oxidation.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Guava (Psidium guajava L.) leaves have been used across Indonesia and globally for traditional remedies and contain a rich profile of bioactive secondary metabolites including tannins, flavonoids (quercetin, kaempferol), phenolic acids (gallic, caffeic), and terpenoids. These molecules display antioxidative, antimicrobial, and metal-chelating properties that are valuable for applications extending beyond health and food into industrial corrosion and mineral protection. In mining and chemical processing, pyrite (FeS2) is a common feedstock and is prone to oxidation when exposed to oxygen and water, producing acidic effluents and mobilizing Fe and S species; inexpensive, non-toxic inhibitors that slow oxidation are therefore of practical interest to reduce environmental impact and processing losses.

Prior research has established the antioxidant and corrosion-inhibition potential of plant extracts including guava leaf extract (GLE) in aqueous media [1][4][11]. Several extraction methods—maceration, Soxhlet and ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE)—yield different profiles and concentrations of active molecules; UAE in particular accelerates extraction kinetics and improves yield [9][10]. Microencapsulation has emerged as a strategy to stabilize bioactive extracts against environmental stress (pH, temperature, light) and to control release rates [12][14]. Ionic gelation of chitosan with STTP is a low-temperature, solvent-minimal route suitable for lab and pilot-scale production, and has been demonstrated for food and pharmaceutical actives [12][13][14].

Despite these advances, a practical gap remains for translating GLE inhibition into mineral protection: unencapsulated extracts leach rapidly under oxidative leaching conditions and produce transient protection, while encapsulation parameters (extract loading, chitosan:STTP ratio, pH) substantially affect particle size, homogeneity, and release. Few studies link systematic variation of extract loading to quantitative changes in particle size, PDI, and inhibitory performance against pyrite oxidation measured by ICP-OES. This gap prevents reliable upscaling and specification of working concentrations for field or industrial laboratory use.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related literature on extraction, encapsulation, and mineral inhibition. Section III describes materials, ultrasonic extraction, ionic-gelation microencapsulation procedure, and characterization methods. Section IV presents experimental results: XRF and FTIR fingerprints, particle size and PDI trends, and leaching test outcomes with ICP-OES analysis. Section V analyzes optimization tradeoffs and provides a discussion on mechanism and limitations. Section VI concludes and outlines specific future work on field trials and accelerated aging.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section summarizes prior work on guava leaf extraction, chitosan ionic-gelation microencapsulation, and plant-extract-based inhibition of oxidation and corrosion. The review highlights methodological differences, limitations in stability or leaching, and gaps addressed by the present study.

section2a.title: Guava Leaf Extraction and Active Composition

content.text: Guava leaf phytochemistry has been extensively profiled in recent reviews and analytical studies [1][2]. Methods such as maceration in aqueous ethanol (30%–70%) and Soxhlet extraction yield different distributions of tannins and phenolics; yields vary with solvent polarity and temperature [6][8]. Ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE) concentrates energy via cavitation and accelerates mass transfer, often producing higher extractable polyphenol content in reduced time and with lower solvent usage [9][10]. A practical limitation of many maceration studies is incomplete reporting of process energy and probe parameters; probe-based UAE (20 kHz, variable amplitude) focuses acoustic energy and can be scaled to bench-top homogenizers as used in this work. In addition, the presence of mineral residues and trace metals in leaf material is rarely quantified in inhibitor literature, yet such elements can influence electrochemical behavior when extracts are applied to mineral surfaces. XRF and ICP-OES complement organic analysis by confirming absence of toxic metals such as Pb and providing oxide-level fractions (see Table I). While reviews suggest strong antioxidant potential, few works provide direct leaching inhibition metrics on sulfide minerals in standardized oxidative baths, and those that do often omit encapsulation steps that would control release [1][3][5].

content.text: Fig. 1 places the extraction and encapsulation steps into a single schematic so readers can trace sample flow from leaf powder through ultrasonication, concentration, chitosan mixing, STTP crosslinking, and characterization. The figure emphasizes instrument parameters that materially affect yield and capsule properties (probe frequency, power, temperature and stirring rates) and serves as a practical recipe for replication in similar university laboratories.

Chitosan is a deacetylated biopolymer with cationic amine groups that form electrostatic complexes with polyanions such as STTP. Ionic gelation protocols prepare chitosan solutions in dilute acetic acid and add STTP to trigger instantaneous crosslinking and nanoparticle formation. Several groups have demonstrated encapsulation of plant extracts (mango, grape, alginate blends) using similar stoichiometries and process controls [11][12][21]. Major variables are chitosan concentration, chitosan:STTP mass ratio, dropwise addition rate, stirring rate, pH at neutralization, and post-processing such as washing and aging. Particle size and homogeneity (PDI) are sensitive to these variables: lower chitosan viscosity and faster STTP addition typically produce smaller particles, but at the cost of reduced encapsulation efficiency. A technical tradeoff remains between high extract loading for efficacy and particle stability: overloaded matrices may aggregate or produce broad size distributions with $\mathrm{PDI}>0.5$. This work systematically varies extract loading while holding chitosan mass (320 mg) and STTP volume (40 ml) fixed to isolate the effect of loading on particle properties.

Mechanistically, initial adsorption of polyphenolic substances onto protonated chitosan chains is followed by STTP-induced crosslinking via phosphate–amine electrostatic pairing. The binding is stronger than hydrogen bonding, producing a three-dimensional network that entraps the active molecules. Previous work has modeled crosslinking kinetics qualitatively but seldom linked kinetics to release behavior under oxidative leaching; we therefore include a simple kinetic model in Section III to relate crosslinking degree to release rate.

section2c.title: Plant Extracts for Mineral Oxidation Inhibition

content.text: Research into natural inhibitors for metal and sulfide oxidation has used tannin-rich extracts, green tea, and agricultural wastes. Guava leaf extract specifically has been demonstrated to reduce corrosion rates in chloride media and to show antioxidant scavenging that can passivate metal surfaces [4][5][11]. Prior studies often report inhibition efficiency as a percent reduction in corrosion current or lower mass loss, but direct chemical monitoring of oxidation products (S and Fe concentrations) via ICP-OES provides a more specific assessment of pyrite dissolution. Comparisons across studies are complicated by differences in test solution composition, temperature, and exposure time. For pyrite, oxidative dissolution often proceeds through multi-step electrochemical and chemical reactions sensitive to pH and oxidant species; an effective inhibitor must form a physical barrier and/or change local electrochemistry to slow electron transfer. Microencapsulation adds a secondary mechanism: controlled release of inhibitor molecules over time, preserving functional groups that complex iron or scavenge radicals.

Finally, sustainability and safety concerns motivate the use of non-toxic matrices (chitosan) and renewable extracts. Nevertheless, scale-up barriers include solvent recovery, batch-to-batch variability in leaf chemistry, and the need to confirm long-term adhesion of coatings on mineral surfaces under field-like agitation. Our study documents reproducible lab-scale processing parameters and direct ICP-OES leaching outcomes to provide quantitative guidance for applied deployment.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section details materials, ultrasonic extraction parameters, ionic gelation protocols, characterization methods (XRF, FTIR, PSA, ICP-OES), and the pyrite leaching assay. Emphasis is placed on reproducible operational parameters used at the Diponegoro University laboratories.

content.text: Materials used include fresh guava leaves sourced from the Diponegoro University campus garden (collected June 2025), analytical grade 96% ethanol (Merck), chitosan (medium molecular weight, degree of deacetylation 75%–85%), glacial acetic acid (Sigma Aldrich), sodium tripolyphosphate (STTP, technical grade), NaOH (1 M, Merck) for pH adjustment, and Milli-Q distilled water. Instruments were an Ultrasonic Homogenizer probe (20 kHz, 200 W, Sonics Vibra-Cell), Vacuum Rotavapor (40 °C setpoint), Magnetic stirrer (300 rpm), Oven (40 °C drying), Malvern Zetasizer Nano ZS for PSA and PDI, Shimadzu FTIR, PANalytical XRF, and PerkinElmer ICP-OES for elemental quantification. All masses, volumes and times were recorded to the nearest mg, mL and minute to ensure reproducibility.

The ICP-OES detection limit of $0.01$ mg/L and PSA lower detection near $0.3$ nm were prerequisites for the study objectives.

section3b.title: Guava Leaf Extraction by Probe Ultrasonication

content.text: Leaves were washed with distilled water, oven-dried at $40\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ until constant mass, and milled to a fine powder using a coffee grinder and a 250 µm sieve. Powder mass $m_{\mathrm{raw}}$ per batch was $100$ g. Powder was soaked in 500 mL of 96% ethanol and sonicated with a probe at $20$ kHz, $200$ W for $60$ minutes in pulse mode (10 s on, 5 s off) to limit heating; temperature was monitored and kept below $35\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The suspension was then filtered and concentrated on a vacuum evaporator at $40\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to yield a viscous extract. The extraction yield was computed by:

where $m_{\mathrm{extract}}$ is the mass of concentrated extract after solvent removal and $m_{\mathrm{raw}}$ is the initial dry leaf powder mass. In our protocol $m_{\mathrm{extract}}$ averaged $10$ g per $100$ g raw powder, giving $Y=10\%$, consistent with yields reported for ethanol-based UAE of tannin-rich leaves [9]. Extract was stored in amber glass at $4\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ until use to minimize oxidation and degradation.

Microencapsulation used a fixed chitosan mass of $320$ mg dissolved in $160$ mL of $1\%$ (v/v) acetic acid. Chitosan solution was stirred at $300$ rpm for $1$ h to ensure complete dissolution. Concentrated GLE was diluted with ethanol and distilled water to target working concentrations $C_{\mathrm{load}} = 500, 1000, 2000, 3500, 5000, 8000$ ppm. The diluted GLE was added dropwise to the chitosan solution while stirring; after 1 h of mixing, $40$ mL of STTP solution was introduced as the cross-linking agent. After another hour, the pH was adjusted to $6$ using $1$ M NaOH. Mixtures were filtered on Whatman filter paper and left $24$ h for phase separation. The ionic-gelation crosslinking can be represented by a simple empirical kinetic relation for degree of crosslinking $X$ as a function of STTP concentration $c$ and time $t$:

where $k$ is an effective rate constant that aggregates mixing and diffusion effects. While this expression is empirical, it provides intuition: higher $c$ or longer $t$ increases crosslinking asymptotically towards unity. For fixed $c$ and $t$ the encapsulation efficiency $\eta$ depends on the available chitosan binding sites and on $C_{\mathrm{load}}$; we measured encapsulation indirectly through particle sizing and leaching performance rather than by chemical quantification of trapped phenolics.

where $m_{\mathrm{added}}$ is the mass of extract added and $m_{\mathrm{encapsulated}}$ approximated from total mass balance post-filtration and wash. Practical encapsulation efficiencies for plant extracts in chitosan reported in the literature range from $40\%$ to $85\%$ depending on matrix composition [12][14].

Characterization comprised XRF for oxide-level mineral composition, FTIR for functional group fingerprinting, PSA for hydrodynamic diameter and PDI, and ICP-OES for elemental release quantification during leaching. Particle size statistics from PSA reported intensity-weighted hydrodynamic diameter and PDI. The De Brouckere volume-weighted mean $D_{[4,3]}$ was used to represent size in certain analyses:
where $d_i$ are bin diameters and $n_i$ counts. Polydispersity index was represented by the squared coefficient of variation:

where $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are the mean and standard deviation of the size distribution respectively; PSA instruments report a derived PDI metric compatible with this concept. Leaching tests used $1\times1\times1$ cm pyrite cubes, cleaned, dried, and dip-coated by immersing samples at $2$ mm/s and withdrawing at the same rate to control film thickness. Coated and uncoated samples were immersed in an oxidative solution (simulant HCl-like oxidative bath, pH adjusted to 3.5 to accelerate oxidation) for $48$ hours (two sequential 24 h periods). Released S and Fe concentrations were measured by ICP-OES; concentration $C$ was calculated from measured mass in solution $m_s$ and volume $V$:

All numerical results quoted in subsequent sections are averages of triplicate samples unless stated otherwise; standard deviations are reported with tables and error bars in figures to maintain transparency.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: This section reports extract composition (XRF and FTIR), microcapsule physical properties as a function of $C_{\mathrm{load}}$, and leaching results quantified by ICP-OES. Data are presented with statistical descriptors and compared to selected literature benchmarks.

content.text: The concentrated guava leaf extract was dark green–black and viscous, consistent with polyphenol-rich concentrates. Extraction yield $Y$ computed from (1) was $10\%$ (mass basis). XRF analysis identified oxide-level mineral fractions summarized in Table II; the organic fraction (C,H,O) was not detected by XRF but inferred from FTIR peaks and mass balance. Detected mineral oxides included K2O at $1.30\%$, Cl at $0.413\%$, SO3 at $0.236\%$, and trace metal oxides (Fe2O3 $0.0087\%$, CuO $0.0041\%$), indicating negligible heavy-metal contamination. These oxide levels support safe handling for the intended inhibitor application and reduce concerns about introducing toxic metals to the pyrite surface during coating.

content.Title: Mineral Oxides in Guava Leaf Extract (XRF)

content.text: Table II matches the XRF output described earlier and confirms K2O dominance among detected minerals. The balance is assigned to organics and undetected light elements, which are expected given the extraction solvent and concentration method. FTIR scans (Fig. 3) show characteristic polyphenolic and chitosan interactions described below.

content.text: FTIR spectra (Fig. 3) show strong O–H stretching near $3307$ cm$^{-1}$, C=C aromatic vibrations near $1636$ cm$^{-1}$, and C=O signals attributed to catechin-like structures. Post-encapsulation spectra indicate band shifts consistent with hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions between chitosan amine groups and phenolic hydroxyls, supporting successful entrapment without chemical degradation of main functional groups [19][20].

Particle size analysis results for microencapsulated samples at each $C_{\mathrm{load}}$ are summarized in Table III and plotted as distributions in Fig. 4. The data show a non-monotonic dependence of hydrodynamic diameter on $C_{\mathrm{load}}$: at low loading ($500$ ppm) particles were larger and highly polydisperse ($665.8$ nm, PDI $0.908$) indicative of unstable nucleation and probable agglomeration. At $1000$ ppm the size increased to $1119$ nm with PDI $0.682$, suggesting aggregation as extract molecules bridge particles. At intermediate loadings $2000$--$3500$ ppm, particle size decreased substantially to $315$ nm (PDI $0.448$) and $390.8$ nm (PDI $0.438$) respectively, indicating more uniform nucleation and stable encapsulation. Higher loading ($5000$ and $8000$ ppm) again increased size and PDI, likely due to saturation of binding sites and excessive hydrophobic interactions promoting aggregation. These trends indicate an optimal loading window where chitosan matrix capacity and extract concentration are balanced.

content.Title: Particle Size and PDI vs. Guava Leaf Extract Loading

content.text: Table III provides the numerical basis for identifying $2000$--$3500$ ppm as the optimized loading range producing particle sizes in the submicron regime with PDI below $0.5$. These values are consistent with prior encapsulation studies of botanical extracts where optimal loading produced particles in the $200$--$500$ nm range that balanced encapsulation efficiency and colloidal stability [21][22][23]. Fig. 4 (particle size distributions) visually corroborates the narrowing of the distribution at $2000$ ppm and $3500$ ppm.

section4c.title: Leaching Test Results: Sulfur and Iron Release

content.text: Leaching tests measured sulfur and iron release after 48 h immersion in oxidative solution. Results are plotted in Fig. 5 and summarized numerically here. Uncoated pyrite released $24.94$ mg/L S and $18.20$ mg/L Fe, confirming rapid oxidation under the chosen bath conditions. Coating with unencapsulated GLE reduced S to $12.54$ mg/L and Fe to $9.45$ mg/L, demonstrating substantive inhibition but limited longevity. Microencapsulated GLE at optimized loading ($2000$ ppm) reduced S to $5.94$ mg/L and Fe to $3.80$ mg/L. Increasing to $3500$ ppm microencapsulated slightly improved numbers to S $5.20$ mg/L and Fe $3.45$ mg/L, suggesting a diminishing return beyond $2000$ ppm. These values are averages of triplicates; standard deviations were below $6\%$ for most groups.

content.text: The leaching results indicate that encapsulation improves long-term inhibition by limiting immediate wash-off and providing a controlled release reservoir. Mechanistically, polyphenolic groups either chelate surface iron, reducing the electrochemical driving force for oxidation, or adsorb to form a hydrophobic film restricting oxidant access. Microcapsules further reduce diffusion of solvent into the active phase, slowing desorption of inhibitor molecules into the bulk solution.

section4d.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation

content.text: We compared the inhibition efficacy and practical metrics of the present microencapsulation with selected literature baselines. Method A (Ngatin et al. [4]) reported inhibition in chloride solutions with efficacy near $72.3\%$; Rehan et al. [11] reported multi-functional alginate/starch microcapsules on cotton with improved durability but did not provide sulfide leaching numbers directly. Costa et al. [21] measured biological activity improvements using polymeric nanoparticles and reported particle sizes similar to our mid-range. To provide a direct, quantitative comparison we computed inhibition efficacy for pyrite oxidation using sulfur release reduction:

Applying the formula with $C_{\mathrm{uncoated}}=24.94$ mg/L and $C_{\mathrm{microencapsulated}}=5.94$ mg/L yields efficacy $\approx 76.2\%$ for the microencapsulated $2000$ ppm coating. For the $3500$ ppm microencapsulated coating efficacy increases to $\approx 79.1\%$. Table V summarizes a head-to-head comparison using inhibition efficacy and an operational latency metric approximating time to stable film formation (related to dip-coating drying and adhesion).

content.text: While some literature entries report higher efficacy under their specific protocols, the present method combines a practical lab-scale recipe, low processing temperature, and measurable suppression of S and Fe release. A practical limitation is that our definition of latency is operational rather than mechanistic; drying times and adhesion depend on substrate roughness and environmental humidity. Additionally, while inhibition efficacy is strong, complete passivation was not achieved, indicating room for optimizing chitosan molecular weight, STTP ratio or post-deposition curing.

Stability under storage was monitored for microcapsule suspensions at $25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $40\%$ relative humidity over 30 days. Particle size drift and PDI growth were small in optimal formulations ($2000$--$3500$ ppm), with size increases below $12\%$ over 30 days and PDI remaining under $0.55$. Time-series data and PDI trends are shown in Fig. 9. These results suggest acceptable shelf stability for short-term storage in amber bottles; however, long-term photo-oxidation and microbial growth were not fully assessed and represent limitations for longer deployments.

content.text: Endurance testing supports the claim that encapsulation increases functional life in storage and under laboratory oxidative exposure. However, a limitation is that abrasion and mechanical loss under field agitation were not simulated; such stresses could compromise coating integrity. Future work should include simulated streamflow or tumbling abrasion tests.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: This study optimized guava leaf extract loading in chitosan–STTP ionic-gelation microcapsules and demonstrated improved inhibition of pyrite oxidation. Ultrasonic probe extraction followed by vacuum concentration yielded extracts with a $10\%$ mass yield and XRF-confirmed low heavy-metal content. Microencapsulation experiments across $C_{\mathrm{load}}=500$ to $8000$ ppm identified an optimal window $2000$--$3500$ ppm producing particle sizes $315$--$390$ nm and $\mathrm{PDI}<0.5$ (Table III). Leaching tests on $1\times1\times1$ cm pyrite cubes in an oxidative bath for $48$ h show sulfur release reductions from $24.94$ mg/L (uncoated) to $5.94$ mg/L (microencapsulated $2000$ ppm) and iron reductions from $18.20$ mg/L to $3.80$ mg/L, corresponding to inhibition efficacies $\approx 76.2\%$ to $79.1\%$ respectively.

The primary technical finding is that moderate extract loadings maximize colloidal stability and inhibition performance: too little extract results in insufficient active concentration; too much extract destabilizes the colloid leading to aggregation and reduced effective coating. The microencapsulation process described here is pragmatic for university laboratories and small pilot plants: it uses commonly available ultrasonic probes, a Malvern Zetasizer for QA, and a PerkinElmer ICP-OES for performance testing.

Limitations include: lack of long-term field abrasion testing and environmental aging under UV exposure, potential variability in leaf chemistry across harvests (batch-to-batch variation), and incomplete chemical quantification of encapsulated phenolics (we used indirect mass-balance and leaching results). Future work includes: (1) controlled field trials with coated pyrite in outdoor weathering plots; (2) analytical quantification of specific phenolic species encapsulated and released over time using HPLC-MS to relate molecule class to inhibition; and (3) scale-up studies addressing solvent recycling, continuous ionic-gelation reactors, and adhesion promoters to improve coating robustness. These steps will help translate the present laboratory optimization into industrially relevant practice for environmentally benign inhibition of sulfide mineral oxidation.
